activity.title: Cleaning out my desk this week brought back some old memories. I stumbled upon a 'relic' from the past - the original, handwritten draft of my first publication by my PhD supervisor. It all happened 16 years ago, when I was sitting in my PhD supervisor’s office with the ChemDraw figures of the publication. In a display of sheer scientific craftsmanship, he drafted the entire manuscript right there on paper, from scratch, in under an hour. -> Mind blown In today’s world of AI and instant digital templates, looking at these ink-stained pages feels like finding a lost art form. There was no auto-correct or copy and pasting. Just pure, unfiltered scientific logic transferring straight from the mind to the page. This scrap of paper is a beautiful reminder that the core of great science remains unchanged: deep focus, compelling storytelling, and the mentors who guide us there. Do you have similar analog relics to share? #BaranLab #Scripps ...more ...more

It's been a remarkably full few months at OpenFold, so we pulled it all into one place: our latest Community Update. Inside this issue: → Eleven new members join the consortium, spanning therapeutic discovery, antibody design, GPCR biology, scientific software, and AI-enabled R&D. → OpenBind's first blind benchmark delivers an encouraging result for OpenFold3, which outperformed AlphaFold3 out of the box, and reached 76% co-folding success after fine-tuning on open fragment-bound structures. → Highlights from our first CoFold Summit in Barcelona, bringing the co-folding community together for talks, panels, and hallway-track problem-solving. → The Rocklin Lab's megascale open protein stability dataset: folding-stability measurements for 1.8 million protein domains, now freely available. → A new research fellowship with the University of Washington's Institute for Protein Design. → Our federated learning keynote panel at Bio-IT World. Every section links out to the full story. Thank you to everyone building open AI for biology alongside us. A strange thing happens to many high-achieving students. At some point they stop studying the subject...and then start studying themselves. A strange shift happens. Chemistry, calculus, literature, and math slowly stop being the source of stress. The student's relationship with themselves becomes the real battlefield. Too many questions nagging at students, with a constant roaring of inner voices such as how much have I finished?how much has she finished? Am I behind or why am I tired already? and some of them become harsher, becoming self- accusatory ..Shouldn't I be working harder? What if everyone else is handling this better than I am? After years of working with IB and AP students, I've noticed something interesting. The students who struggle the most are not always the ones with the hardest courses nor with the weakest foundations.. Sometimes they're the students who spend the entire day watching themselves learn, constantly evaluating, measuring, second-guessing themselves. After delving into neuroscience, I now understand better. The brain doesn't really distinguish between solving a problem and worrying about the problem. In fact, both consume mental resources. This means while a student is trying to learn electrochemistry, part of their attention is busy asking "am I behind?" same for Literature too. While they're reading Shakespeare, another part is wondering, what score will this get me? At some point, the subject is no longer the main workload but self-monitoring is. Here is the problem - this kind of exhaustion is particularly cruel because it looks like laziness from the outside. Perhaps with a student sitting at the desk, books open, ipad is on but t half of their energy is being spent managing anxiety rather than learning. One of the most helpful things(hopefully) I tell my students during exam season is that they don't need to monitor yourself every minute to be a responsible student. Nor do they need to constantly calculate their worth through productivity. Perhaps the most productive thing a student can do is stop asking whether they do "enough" and return to the next page. The next question. that next small step. Because learning requires attention. unfortunately, attention is expensive. Meaning? the more of it we spend watching ourselves, the less of it remains for the thing we are actually trying to learn. ...more ...more

💡 Proteins aren't static – they constantly shift between different shapes, and those motions are often essential to their function. Yet, many AI structure prediction models collapse this complexity into a single "best" structure. We are excited to share a new study, co-authored by Eric and Wendy Schmidt Center postdoctoral fellow Sanketh Vedula , which addresses this long-standing challenge. Published in Nature Biotechnology, this work introduces experiment-guided AlphaFold3, a framework that integrates experimental data from techniques such as NMR, X-ray crystallography, and cryo-EM into AlphaFold3 to reconstruct ensembles of protein structures that better reflect biological reality. By capturing structural heterogeneity rather than a single conformation, the approach opens new possibilities for studying protein dynamics, advancing inverse protein design, and accelerating drug discovery. Congratulations to Sanketh, and co-authors Advaith Sai , Nadav Bojan Sellam , Meital Bojan , Volodymyr Masalitin , Paul Schanda , Ailie Marx , and Alex Bronstein on this exciting milestone, and to collaborators at the Institute of Science and Technology Austria (ISTA), TEL HAI Academic College , MIGAL Galilee Research Institute , Princeton University , and the Schmidt Center at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard . The team’s follow-up study is going to be presented at #ICML2026 , which introduces a general inference-time optimization framework that addresses limitations in the reverse‑diffusion process, and results in consistently more accurate experiment-grounded ensembles. #ProteinStructure #AlphaFold #StructuralBiology #AIinBiology #MachineLearning Nature Portfolio ...more ...more

I’m happy to share that I’ve started a new chapter in my teaching journey at International Programs School (IPS) International Programs School in Al Khobar, Saudi Arabia, as a Mathematics Teacher. After two memorable years at King’s Academy King's Academy in Jordan, it feels exciting to begin again in a new school, a new country, and a new community. I’m looking forward to getting to know my students and colleagues, contributing to the mathematics program, and bringing what I’ve learned over the years into this new experience. Grateful for the people and experiences that have been part of my journey so far, and looking forward to what comes next.
Happy to share that I will be joining The D. E. Shaw Group as a Quantitative Research Intern next summer. After that, I will be joining Citadel as a Quantitative Development Intern in the fall.

I am excited to announce that I have successfully completed my research internship at KAIST in the laboratory of Prof. Sunkyu Han, focusing on Natural Product Synthesis. During this period, I had the privilege of gaining hands-on research experience in total synthesis and novel synthetic methodologies. I am deeply grateful to Prof. Sunkyu Han and the entire research team for their guidance, mentorship, and support throughout this incredible journey. Looking forward to the next steps in my scientific career!

A new era for the Turkish student diaspora has begun. We’re not asking for a seat at the table anymore. We’re building one of our own. We are in a global diaspora race. We don’t have a talent problem. We have what it takes. All we need is to bring the right people together to build it and that’s exactly what our team at TSA Global is pushing for. What we are building is much more than speakers and students coming together in the same room. We are building a system where people hold on to each other. Where no one has to step on someone else to climb higher. We push each other up. We open doors for each other. When one of us wins, more of us rise with them. We want to put Türkiye’s name up there. We want “I’m Turkish” to stand for ambition, talent, capability, and the determination to do what it takes. The Istanbul Gala was a big step. But it was only the first one. We are just getting started.

Screw vibe coding. Take matters into your own hands. Every AI model you use is bloated and inefficient. They need trillions of 16 bit weights when only 2 bits can do. That’s why I built my own 2-bit language model by hand. Introducing Avenue, a family of ternary language models that can train on your MacBook. Named after the avenues of East Village, NYC. The best 2-bit model performs better than a full precision model 25% bigger than itself. At scale, a model that needs 8GB would fit in 1GB. All trained on a MacBook Pro in 43 hours. And the best part, I wrote every single line of code by hand, not via an AI agent. That includes a custom tokenizer, a training pipeline with Quantization-aware training (QAT) support, and an inference stack with Post-training Quantization (PTQ) ability. The sample generation below speaks for itself. We see that FP and QAT ternary are close, while PTQ sucks. Doing this was hard. So I’m making it easier for others: I wrote a ~1900 word math explainer on how 2-bit models actually work, everything is open source, and the models are up on HuggingFace. Links in comments. Next step: MLX and a GPT-2 scale model.
